body.heading: Spin remembers a direction
paragraphs: A spinning object has angular momentum, a kind of stubbornness about its axis. Just as a moving object resists changes to its path, a spinning top resists changes to the direction its axle points. That resistance is why the top, balanced on a point, does not simply fall over the moment you let go.

Gravity is pulling the top sideways the whole time, trying to topple it. But instead of falling, the axle responds by swinging slowly around in a small circle — a motion called precession. The faster the spin, the stronger the resistance and the steadier the top stands.

body.heading: Why it wobbles, then falls
paragraphs: Friction is quietly stealing the top's spin from the first second — a little at the tip, a little from the air. As the spin slows, the angular momentum weakens, gravity's toppling gets the upper hand, and the precession widens into the familiar drunken wobble.

At last the axle tilts so far that the side of the top touches the ground, friction grabs it, and the remaining spin drains away in a final clatter. The top did not defy gravity at any point; it just kept postponing the fall for as long as its spin lasted.

body.heading: The top's serious relatives
paragraphs: The same effect steadies a bicycle wheel, a frisbee in flight and a rifled bullet. Engineers build it into gyroscopes: precisely spun wheels whose fixed axes let aircraft, ships and spacecraft measure which way they have turned, even with no view of the sky.

Earth itself is a spinning top. The pull of the Sun and Moon on our planet's equatorial bulge makes its axis precess in a slow circle that takes about 26,000 years to complete — so the star that marks our north pole slowly changes over the millennia.
